title: Change Exposed Passwords and Stop Reusing Them
body_md:
If account credentials were included in this breach, change the affected password promptly. This applies even when passwords were exposed in hashed (scrambled) form, since hashed passwords can sometimes be recovered.

1. Sign in to the affected account and set a new password. If you cannot sign in, use the service's account-recovery process.
2. Change the same password anywhere else you used it. Reused passwords let a single exposure open other accounts.
3. Make each new password long — at least 12 characters — and unique to that account. A phrase of several unrelated words works well.
4. Consider a password manager, which generates and stores a distinct password for every account.
5. Update security questions on the affected account if their answers may also have been exposed.

Prioritize email accounts: an email account can be used to reset passwords on most other accounts. Then move to financial, medical, and government accounts. Federal guidance on creating strong passwords is at consumer.ftc.gov/articles/creating-strong-passwords-and-other-ways-protect-your-accounts.
